title: Hide Artifacts
summary: Hide artifacts is a defensive evasion technique that covers the many ways an adversary conceals the traces of their activity instead of removing the activity itself. Operating systems provide legitimate concealment features so that system files, administrative execution, and management accounts do not clutter or disrupt the user environment, and those same features can be turned against the defender. Files, directories, accounts, scheduled tasks, and other objects can all be made invisible to the standard tools a responder reaches for first, which means an investigation that relies on default views can finish with a clean bill of health and still be wrong. The technique also extends beyond naming conventions and attributes to isolation: behaviour performed inside a virtualised region, a lightweight container, or another boundary that ordinary host instrumentation does not observe can be effectively hidden without anything on the visible file system being altered at all. Defenders counter this by understanding exactly which mechanism reduces visibility, and by collecting the lower level evidence that the mechanism does not affect. A hidden attribute suppresses a directory listing but does not prevent a file creation event, an account hidden from the logon screen still exists in the account database, and an object hidden from a graphical interface still appears in the raw configuration store. The unifying detection principle is to enumerate from the authoritative source rather than the convenient display, and to baseline those enumerations so that differences stand out.

beginner.definition: This technique is about an attacker hiding the traces of what they did. They do not delete the evidence, they make it hard to see. A file, a folder, or an account can be marked so that normal lists do not show it. Some attackers also hide activity inside a virtual machine, where ordinary security tools cannot watch. It is a way of avoiding detection rather than a way of breaking in.
beginner.whyItMatters: When you investigate a computer, you look at the files, accounts, and tasks it lists. If an attacker can remove items from those lists, your investigation finds nothing and you conclude the machine is clean. You may then rebuild the computer without removing the cause, so the problem returns. Some hiding methods are switched on by a single system setting, so the attacker does not even need special software. Knowing each hiding method is the only way to check for it properly.
howItWorks: The attacker places something on the machine, such as a file, folder, task, or account.
They then change how that item is recorded so common tools stop listing it.
The change may be a name, a file attribute, a registry value, or an account setting.
The item keeps working normally even though it is missing from the usual display.
Some attackers go further and run their activity inside a virtual area instead.
Defenders must query the underlying store directly instead of trusting the display.
beginner.example: Picture an office where each desk has a labelled tray for incoming post. A worker adds a document to the pile but prints the label in a colour that matches the tray. The document is still there and still processed, yet anyone glancing at the tray sees nothing unusual. Only a person who reads every single sheet, rather than trusting the labels, finds it.
takeaways: Hiding hides the evidence of activity, so an empty result is not proof of safety.
Each hiding method needs a different countermeasure and a different data source.
Baselines and direct queries beat trusting what a normal interface shows you.

objectives: Define artifact hiding and explain why it is classified as defence evasion.
Describe why legitimate operating system features can be abused to hide activity.
List several kinds of artifact an adversary may hide, such as files, accounts, or tasks.
Explain how virtualisation or isolation can conceal behaviour from host based tools.
Describe how to enumerate objects from an authoritative source instead of a default view.
Explain why baselines make hidden artifacts easier to spot over time.
